## Intent
Hypothesis: compiler auto-vectorization of the integrate loop can compensate for the AoS stride-68 layout's poor hot-byte fraction and lift overall throughput toward the streaming ceiling.

## Layout & approach
The 68 B/particle AoS structure offers three loops wildly different hot fractions: loop 1 touches 24/68 B (35%), loop 2 only 8/68 B (11%), loop 3 touches 28/68 B (41%) — the remaining bytes are dead weight dragged through every cache line. No intermediate storage means the death verdict stays in registers, avoiding a second pass, but it also means each loop re-walks the full 68 B stride. Auto-vectorization targets loop 1 only; loops 2 and 3 remain scalar and branchy. With working-set spills at N≈481 (L1d), N≈7710 (L2), and N≈246723 (L3), the 11%-hot loop 2 is the most wasteful in bandwidth terms, but its branchy RNG logic makes it the compute bottleneck regardless.

## Cache saturation
At q=0.01 the ns/p curve is nearly flat across L1d and L2 regimes: 22.0 at N=320, rising only to 25.1 at N=7700 — a 14% increase over a 24× working-set growth, confirming the algo is not cache-bound in these regimes. The L3 regime (N=10000–160000) holds steady at ~24.5–25.5 ns/p. The only visible knee is the L3→DRAM spill at N≈250000, where ns/p steps from 24.5 to 26.6 (q=0.01) — a 9% rise that the dense grid resolves cleanly. At q=0.5 the curve is even flatter (33.7→37.1 across all N), because loop 2/3 overhead grows with death rate and masks cache effects entirely. The memory floor of 5.36 ns/p sits 4–7× below every measured point, so cache pressure is never the governing constraint.

## Bandwidth
Achieved bandwidth peaks at 3.1 GB/s (q=0.01, L1d) — 24% of the 12.69 GB/s ceiling — and decays to 1.8 GB/s at q=0.5 in DRAM. Against the 5.36 ns/p floor, the algo spends <25% of its time on irreducible memory traffic; the rest is compute, branch, and overhead. Backend stalls dominate at 60–71% across all profiles, with branch_flush at 10–15%. The verdict is compute-and-branch-bound, not bandwidth-bound, at every N×q. Ratios vs the scalar baseline are ~1.0× throughout — 0.98–1.02× in cache at q=0.01, rising only to 1.08–1.16× in DRAM — meaning the auto-vectorized loop 1 yields no net gain over scalar. Against the winner (AF02.LP1-autovec.LP2-opt), the algo is 2.97–3.6× slower at q=0.01 and still 2.0× slower at q=0.5; the gap is widest in L3 (3.6× at N=160000) where the winner's optimized LP2 streams but this algo's simple LP2 stalls.

## Assembly
Loop 1 shows partial vectorization: `vmovups` loads 16 B from the stride-68 structure, `vshufps`/`vinsertps` rearrange components, and `vmulps`/`vaddps` do 4-wide FP — but 3 of 9 FP ops remain scalar (`vmulss`, `vaddss`, `vsubss`), because the 3-component pos+vel layout doesn't fill lanes. Loop 2 (75 insns, 13 cond branches) is entirely scalar: `vucomiss` for the death check, `xor`/`rorx`/`imul` for RNG mixing, and a `call` to `spawn` — the branchy `jae`→call path blocks any vectorization. Loop 3 (199 insns, 21 cond branches) is the heaviest: 12 `cmovae` selects for byte clamping and 16 byte-granular stores (`mov BYTE PTR`) form the pixel scatter, each channel requiring a `movzx`→`add`→`cmp`→`cmovae`→`mov byte` chain. Only 15/367 instructions are vector-suffixed; loop 1's partial vectorization is swamped by the scalar loops 2–3 that drive the 60–71% backend stalls.

## Verdict
Refuted — the algo runs at 0.98–1.16× of the naive scalar baseline at every N×q point, never pulling ahead: loop 1's partial vectorization (15 vec insns of 367) cannot offset the scalar branchy loop 2 (75 insns, 13 branches) and the byte-scatter loop 3 (199 insns, 16 byte stores). At q=0.01 it is 2.97–3.6× slower than the winner, widening in L3 where the winner's optimized LP2 streams but this algo's simple LP2 stalls at 24% of ceiling. At q=0.5 the winner gap narrows to ~2.0× because respawn overhead dominates both, yet the algo still matches rather than beats baseline. The 4–7× gap above the 5.36 ns/p memory floor confirms the bottleneck is compute and branch, not bandwidth, and auto-vectorizing one loop in a three-loop AoS pipeline with 11–41% hot-byte fractions cannot rescue throughput.
